paragraphs: This paper asks when a graph neural network can lose many parameters while retaining its ability to distinguish graph structures. Earlier expressive lottery-ticket results concerned static graphs. The authors extend that perspective to networks handling multiple relationship types and temporal information, using relational Weisfeiler–Leman expressivity as the standard for what the network can distinguish.

The main result establishes that sufficiently parameterized relational graph neural networks contain sparse subnetworks preserving 1-RWL expressivity. It also gives a lower bound on the probability of finding such a subnetwork through random pruning. The parameterization condition matters: the result does not say that arbitrary pruning of any network will preserve its expressive capabilities.

The authors show that common temporal networks and cross-graph message-passing schemes can be reformulated as relational networks, allowing them to inherit the guarantees. They also connect sparse-network expressivity with optimization under common update regimes. Experiments compare the probability bound with synthetic observations and examine relationships between initial expressivity, optimization, and prediction quality on temporal and molecular tasks.
icml-2026-a-unifying-relational-perspect.tldr: The paper establishes conditional expressivity guarantees and random-pruning probability bounds for sparse relational and temporal graph networks.

paragraphs: Knowledge in a neural network is distributed across parameters, making an individual learned memory difficult to identify. This paper asks whether identifiable memory traces can nevertheless be recovered. It introduces AI engrams through a geometric framework that translates four biological memory criteria—specificity, reactivation, sufficiency, and necessity—into a constrained inverse problem.

The authors derive a closed-form estimator for isolating individual traces from entangled parameters. They show that the resulting solution corresponds to a natural gradient update on the parameter manifold, connecting the biological criteria to the geometry of parameter changes. This provides a mathematical account of how a particular memory can have a specific function despite being stored within a distributed system.

The framework supports combining or erasing subsets of identified memories through linear arithmetic, without iterative optimization. Experiments spanning simple multilayer perceptrons and large language models demonstrate causal validity and substantial scalability. The contribution is therefore both an account of memory organization and a method for manipulating learned knowledge through the traces that the framework identifies.
icml-2026-ai-engram-in-search-of-memory-.tldr: AI Engram uses a geometric framework to isolate memory traces and combine or erase them through linear parameter operations.

paragraphs: Strong text-to-image models can produce high-quality images that follow a prompt while still generating overly similar results across different random seeds. This paper investigates how that similarity develops inside Transformer-based models trained with flow objectives. Its focus is the early generation process, where initially different trajectories can begin converging before much visual variation has developed.

The authors examine intermediate features and identify a rapidly converging spatial-average component, also called the zero-frequency or DC component. They associate this convergence with early trajectory lock-in that restricts later variation. Their method, DAVE, selectively weakens that component during the early generation regime, intervening directly in the model’s internal representations.

DAVE requires no training and preserves the existing sampling pipeline with negligible overhead. The reported result is greater diversity among images that remain consistent with the prompt, while image quality stays competitive. The approach matters because it targets an observed internal source of homogeneity without relying on the expensive sampling or auxiliary optimization used by other diversity-enhancement approaches.
icml-2026-breaking-the-lock-in-diversify.tldr: DAVE improves prompt-consistent image diversity by weakening an early spatial-average feature component, without training and with negligible overhead.

paragraphs: Sparse principal component analysis seeks dominant directions of variation that involve only a small number of coordinates. Simple combinatorial methods are attractive, but their guarantees have typically relied on the restrictive spiked identity covariance model. This paper investigates what happens when the covariance has a more general structure while its leading eigenvector remains sparse.

The authors construct explicit covariance examples on which standard combinatorial approaches fail outside that model. They then provide a combinatorial method with a global convergence guarantee for the truncated power method. For a leading eigenvector with s nonzero coordinates in dimension d, the stated sample requirement is polynomial in s and log(d), and runtime is d squared times such a polynomial.

This establishes a route to general-covariance guarantees using a combinatorial approach, addressing a gap with methods based on semidefinite programming. The authors also extend the method to recovering multiple sparse principal components and evaluate it on synthetic and real datasets. The central contribution is the theoretical expansion beyond the spiked identity setting, supported by empirical evaluation.
icml-2026-combinatorial-sparse-pca-beyon.tldr: The paper gives a provably successful combinatorial sparse PCA method for general covariance structures beyond the spiked identity model.

paragraphs: Removing unwanted visual concepts from an image generator is difficult when the goal also includes preserving image quality. This paper introduces an internal intervention for modern diffusion and autoregressive image models, including SD3.5, Flux, and Infinity. It targets a bottleneck layer shared by the models under study as a place to control concept-specific signals.

The method replaces that layer with a transcoder trained to reproduce its behavior while organizing activations into distinct features. Selected features can then be disabled to suppress particular concepts while preserving the remaining model behavior. Because the replacement becomes part of the model backbone, the intervention persists when users have white-box access, rather than depending on a separately attached filtering component.

The authors report state-of-the-art concept removal across the evaluated diffusion and autoregressive models, alongside maintained visual quality and robustness against adversarial prompts. They also demonstrate sequential removal of different concepts. These findings support the method as a practical way to embed selective concept filtering within the generator itself.
icml-2026-concept-removal-for-frontier-i.tldr: Replacing an internal bottleneck with a feature-structured transcoder enables selective concept removal while preserving image quality in evaluated frontier generators.

paragraphs: Some statistical responses live on curved spaces rather than ordinary flat coordinate spaces. Geodesic regression extends linear regression to this setting by modeling responses on a Riemannian manifold. Its fitted parameters can describe relationships involving sensitive data, so publishing those parameters raises a privacy question even when the original observations are not released.

This paper develops a method for releasing geodesic regression parameters with differential privacy using the K-Norm Gradient mechanism on manifolds. The authors derive theoretical sensitivity bounds and connect them to Jacobi fields, geometric quantities describing variation among geodesics. Consequently, the curvature of the underlying space enters the analysis of how sensitive the released parameters are.

The method is demonstrated on a sphere, the space of symmetric positive definite matrices, and Kendall’s planar shape space. These examples illustrate its applicability across different nonlinear geometries. The authors present the methodology as general to Riemannian manifolds, making it relevant to settings such as medical imaging and computer vision where geometric data and privacy concerns can coexist.
icml-2026-differentially-private-geodesi.tldr: The paper develops differentially private geodesic regression and shows how parameter sensitivity depends on the geometry of the data space.

paragraphs: Researchers use the geometry of language-model weights to interpret model behavior, but its value for predicting task performance is less clear. This paper studies the unembedding matrix, especially its effective rank, across 108 OLMo-style models trained with controlled variations. The aim is to separate relationships with performance from relationships introduced by training choices.

The best models often have high effective rank, but that pattern does not hold across all tasks and training settings. The experiments also challenge the claim that low effective rank causes late-stage performance degradation in small models. The authors find cases where low rank occurs without performance saturation, indicating that the two phenomena can coincide without the proposed causal relationship.

Batch size and weight decay strongly influence effective rank and also affect performance. Other geometric measurements and final-layer representation metrics largely agree with one another, yet none reliably predicts downstream performance in the study. The findings suggest that these existing measurements primarily reflect how a model was trained, making them unreliable stand-ins for evaluating its actual task capabilities.
icml-2026-disentangling-geometry-perform.tldr: Across 108 controlled language-model variants, existing geometric metrics reflect training choices more reliably than downstream performance.

paragraphs: Rules that guide one language model may not produce a stable society of interacting agents. This paper studies that problem in a grid-world simulation with survival pressure. It evaluates constitutions—behavioral rules for agents—using a Societal Stability Score that combines productivity, survival, and conflict, exposing tension between individual behavior and collective welfare.

The proposed Constitutional Evolution framework uses language-model-driven genetic programming with multiple evolving populations to discover interpretable rules. The objective rewards social welfare without explicitly directing the search toward cooperation. Adversarial rules produce collapse, vague prosocial rules achieve a score of 0.249, and rules designed by an objective-informed Claude 4.5 Opus achieve 0.332.

The evolved constitution reaches 0.556 ± 0.008, reported as 123% higher than human-designed baselines across ten runs, and eliminates conflict. It also sharply reduces social actions: 0.9% compared with 62.2%, with less communication outperforming verbose coordination in this setting. The results show that effective cooperative norms can emerge through optimization in the simulation rather than needing to be specified beforehand.
icml-2026-evolving-interpretable-constit.tldr: Evolutionary search discovers interpretable agent rules that improve simulated social welfare, eliminate conflict, and favor minimal communication.

paragraphs: Neural networks remain vulnerable to natural input corruptions, including models beyond traditional convolutional architectures. This paper investigates that vulnerability through internal features. The authors observe that corruption often pushes the feature space into a high-entropy collapsed state, leaving predictions dependent on a small set of fragile features. That observation motivates a targeted way to fine-tune robustness.

Their method, Dem-HEC, generates high-entropy examples within a bounded perturbation region. It then fine-tunes the model using both these examples and clean inputs, addressing the problematic feature behavior while preserving performance on uncorrupted data. A knowledge-distillation objective from a teacher snapshot helps maintain stable predictions during this repair process.

The authors report effectiveness across datasets with different image resolutions and across convolutional networks, Transformers, and foundation models including DinoV3. Their evaluations show improvements over state-of-the-art approaches in corruption robustness while retaining or improving clean accuracy. The significance is that the observed internal failure pattern becomes a training signal, allowing robustness and ordinary predictive performance to be addressed together.
icml-2026-feature-collapse-under-corrupt.tldr: Dem-HEC uses entropy-guided fine-tuning to improve natural-corruption robustness while retaining or improving clean accuracy.

paragraphs: A nonlinear time-series model can learn relationships whose direction and strength change with the current state. Summarizing each relationship with one number can hide those changes. This paper argues that the more informative object is a response function describing how influence varies across magnitudes, regimes, and contexts, rather than a single score attached to an edge.

The authors formalize this perspective for additive architectures whose contributions can be separated. Using Neural Additive Vector Autoregression, they develop a practical method based on Individual Conditional Expectation to extract response functions from trained models. Their analysis shows how scalar summaries can mix variation between states with residual noise within a state, losing distinctions the nonlinear model has learned.

Controlled synthetic experiments show that indistinguishable edge scores can conceal monotonic, thresholded, saturating, or sign-changing effects. A democratic-development case study also reveals regime-specific and asymmetric relationships missed by score-centered analysis. The contribution is a way to inspect the functional structure of learned causal influence within the stated architectural setting.
icml-2026-function-valued-causal-influen.tldr: Function-valued analysis reveals state-dependent causal relationships that single-number edge scores can obscure in nonlinear time-series models.

paragraphs: Answering questions about long contexts usually requires a Transformer to retain a large cache of past activations. GradMem studies an alternative: compress the context into a small memory and answer after the original context has been removed. This setting makes the quality of the memory-writing operation central, because the model cannot consult the source text during answering.

GradMem writes information by taking a few gradient-descent steps on a small set of prefix memory tokens while keeping the model’s weights fixed. The optimization minimizes a self-supervised context-reconstruction loss. This gives the writing process an explicit error signal and repeated opportunities to correct its memory representation, rather than producing the memory solely through forward computation.

On associative key–value retrieval, GradMem outperforms forward-only writers at the same memory size. Additional gradient steps also increase capacity more effectively than repeated forward writes. With pretrained language models, the method achieves competitive results on natural-language tasks including bAbI and SQuAD variants, using only information stored in the compact memory.
icml-2026-gradmem-learning-to-write-cont.tldr: GradMem compresses context into prefix memory tokens through test-time gradient descent, enabling answers after the original context is removed.

paragraphs: When a language model states its confidence, it is unclear whether it computes that judgment on demand or retrieves an evaluation formed while answering. This paper investigates both the timing and content of verbal confidence. The study focuses on Gemma 3 27B, Qwen 2.5 7B, and Magistral Small 24B, with Gemma examined across factual, mathematical, and general-knowledge tasks.

Several interventions on internal activations provide converging evidence for cached retrieval. Confidence-related representations appear near the answer before reaching the position where confidence is verbalized. Attention-blocking experiments trace a path in which information is gathered from answer tokens, stored at the first position after the answer, and later retrieved to produce the confidence statement.

Linear probes and variance analysis show that these cached representations explain substantial confidence variation beyond token log-probabilities. This supports an interpretation involving richer answer-quality evaluation rather than fluency alone. In the studied models, verbal confidence therefore appears to draw on an automatically formed self-evaluation, with implications for understanding model metacognition and improving calibration.
icml-2026-how-do-llms-compute-verbal-con.tldr: Experiments suggest that studied LLMs cache confidence during answering and later retrieve an evaluation richer than token probabilities alone.

paragraphs: Data pricing differs from pricing ordinary goods because multiple buyers can benefit from the same dataset simultaneously. Standard supply-meets-demand reasoning therefore does not transfer directly. This paper introduces a data-pricing equilibrium based on Nash equilibrium and examines how the answer changes depending on whether datasets complement one another or can substitute for one another.

The authors study complementary data through Leontief utilities and substitutable data through linear utilities. The distinction has major consequences: equilibrium prices can fail to exist with linear utilities even for homogeneous buyers and only two sellers. For Leontief utilities, they establish existence, efficiency, and polynomial-time computation guarantees in general markets with homogeneous buyers and multiple sellers.

The paper also examines how platform mediation and price discrimination can enable optimal equilibrium outcomes to be computed efficiently. Its proof approach uses a graph of deviations to systematically narrow the set of candidate equilibria. Together, the results show that the structure of buyers’ preferences is central to whether a stable and efficiently computable data-pricing arrangement is available.
icml-2026-how-to-price-data-a-market-equ.tldr: A Nash-based data-pricing framework yields strong guarantees for complementary-data utilities, while equilibrium can fail for substitutable-data utilities.

paragraphs: Language models sometimes exhibit recognizable reasoning behaviors, but ordinary sampling may rarely produce more complex combinations of them. Standard reinforcement learning consequently may not reliably teach a diverse repertoire. This paper proposes structured reasoning: deliberately exploring particular reasoning patterns during training so that useful behaviors have a better opportunity to be discovered and reinforced.

Ctrl-R implements this idea by actively guiding rollout trajectories. Its behavior policy supports accurate importance-sampling estimation, enabling unbiased on-policy optimization despite the controlled exploration. The framework additionally introduces a power-scaling factor for the importance weights, allowing selective learning from exploratory trajectories outside the usual distribution while maintaining stable optimization.

Experiments on mathematical reasoning show effective exploration and internalization of patterns described as previously unattainable, with consistent improvements across language and vision–language models. The approach matters because it treats the distribution of reasoning trajectories as something training can deliberately shape. The reported gains connect targeted exploration with learning those behaviors into the model, rather than merely producing unusual trajectories during sampling.
icml-2026-learning-structured-reasoning-.tldr: Ctrl-R guides reinforcement-learning rollouts toward diverse reasoning patterns and reports consistent mathematical-reasoning improvements across language and vision–language models.

paragraphs: Users can express the same goal in many different ways, and small wording differences should not necessarily change a model’s response. Conversely, genuinely different goals should lead to different behavior. This paper turns that distinction into a formal evaluation framework for intent comprehension, addressing the possibility that a model follows surface wording more closely than underlying meaning.

The framework decomposes response variation into three sources: differences in user intent, differences in how an intent is articulated, and model uncertainty. A model showing stronger intent comprehension should attribute more variation to changed intentions and less to alternative wording of the same intention. This provides a semantic diagnostic that ordinary accuracy measurements do not directly capture.

Across diverse domains and five evaluated LLaMA and Gemma models, larger models typically assign a greater share of response variance to intent. However, the improvements with size are uneven and often modest. The results support using this decomposition to assess robustness to rephrasing while keeping the observed relationship between scale and comprehension appropriately qualified.
icml-2026-measuring-intent-comprehension.tldr: A response-variance framework measures whether LLM behavior tracks user intent rather than wording, finding modest and uneven benefits from model scale.

paragraphs: Physiological signals change over time and contain short, localized events that can be difficult for both conventional deep models and neural operators designed around differential equations. NeurOCNN adapts the neural-operator approach to these signals. Its goal is to map an underlying signal function to a label while remaining robust when the signal is sampled at different rates.

The architecture combines continuous-time convolutions parameterized by splines with Fourier projection pooling. The convolutions capture local signal shape, while pooling converts representations of varying size into a fixed-dimensional form. Together, these components support inference that is consistent across discretizations, including sampling-rate changes that were not encountered during training.

The empirical results show stronger performance than standard neural-operator baselines and performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods. Accuracy also remains stable across multiple previously unseen evaluation sampling rates. The contribution is therefore an architecture designed around both localized physiological events and changes in how densely signals are recorded, with the latter tested through zero-shot sampling-rate shifts.
icml-2026-neurocnn-a-neural-operator-bas.tldr: NeurOCNN combines continuous-time convolutions and Fourier pooling to classify physiological signals robustly across previously unseen sampling rates.

paragraphs: Function-guided protein design aims to create proteins from descriptions of what they should do, with applications in drug discovery and enzyme engineering. Comparing models is difficult when studies choose different, limited sets of evaluation criteria. PDFBench addresses this by providing a shared benchmark that evaluates eight models using 16 metrics across two forms of functional guidance.

For description-guided design, the authors repurpose Mol-Instructions, which previously lacked quantitative benchmarking. For keyword-guided design, they introduce SwissTest, a new test set constructed with a strict datetime cutoff to support data integrity. These two settings allow the benchmark to examine models under distinct ways of specifying a desired function.

The benchmark also analyzes correlations among evaluation metrics, helping researchers understand how different criteria relate rather than treating every score as independent. Its main contribution is the evaluation framework: a more consistent basis for model comparisons and for interpreting what different measures reveal. This addresses both fairness across models and the broader problem of understanding performance across multiple aspects of protein design.
icml-2026-pdfbench-a-benchmark-for-de-no.tldr: PDFBench standardizes function-guided protein-design evaluation across eight models, 16 metrics, and description- and keyword-guided tasks.

paragraphs: Early-exit neural networks can stop at an intermediate classifier when a prediction appears sufficiently confident, saving further computation. Because stopping often depends on confidence thresholds, better calibration is commonly expected to improve the overall system. This paper shows that calibration alone is insufficient for making effective use of adaptive computation.

The authors introduce Early-Exit Failure Prediction, or EEFP, which considers both whether a prediction is correct and the cost of continuing computation. That joint perspective matches the decision an early-exit system must make: its usefulness depends on predictive success together with how much computation it spends. A confidence assessment focused only on correctness does not capture that entire trade-off.

The paper also proposes a lightweight procedure, motivated by EEFP, for improving intermediate classifiers that can directly replace calibration. Extensive experiments report better cost–accuracy trade-offs than calibration-based approaches. EEFP also reflects overall early-exit performance more reliably, supporting both a different way to evaluate intermediate predictions and a practical procedure for improving them.
icml-2026-rethinking-calibration-for-ear.tldr: Accounting for correctness and further computation cost improves early-exit decisions beyond what calibration alone provides.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning policy can satisfy safety constraints during training yet encounter different conditions after deployment. This paper examines that gap using diabetes management in a unified clinical simulator. The study asks whether safe RL policies remain safe for unseen patients, making changes in the patient population a direct test of safety generalization.

The benchmark finds that policies meeting training-time constraints frequently violate safety requirements on new patients. The authors then apply test-time shielding, which uses learned dynamics models to filter unsafe actions. This adds a safety intervention at the point of action selection and effectively restores safety across the evaluated algorithms and patient populations.

The evaluation covers eight safe RL algorithms, three diabetes types, and three age groups. For strong baselines including PPO-Lag and CPO, shielding produces reported Time-in-Range gains of 13–14% while reducing clinical risk index and glucose variability. These simulator results identify a concrete generalization problem and establish a shared testbed for studying how deployment-time safeguards address it.
icml-2026-safety-generalization-under-di.tldr: A diabetes simulator exposes safety failures on unseen patients and shows that test-time action shielding improves safety across evaluated safe RL algorithms.

paragraphs: Online multiple testing makes a sequence of decisions while controlling the false discovery rate. Methods based on e-values provide this control under minimal assumptions, but they can lose power by discarding evidence beyond the rejection threshold. SCORE introduces a shared accounting principle for recovering that excess evidence and using it to support subsequent testing.

The framework uses an inequality that separates the contribution needed for a rejection from the amount by which evidence exceeds the threshold. This overshoot becomes a refund rather than being wasted. The authors develop SCORE versions of LOND, LORD, and SAFFRON, proving that these procedures strictly dominate their original counterparts while retaining valid finite-sample false discovery rate control.

Under mild assumptions, SCORE also permits retroactive updates to alpha-wealth, the accounting resource governing testing aggressiveness. The latest decision first determines a reward or loss and then refreshes past wealth. This enables more aggressive tests while preserving error control. Simulations and real-data experiments validate the proposed methods, complementing the theoretical guarantees with evidence of improved statistical power.
icml-2026-score-a-unified-framework-for-.tldr: SCORE recovers excess e-value evidence to improve online testing power while preserving finite-sample false discovery rate control.

paragraphs: Generating a spreadsheet workbook from a natural-language request requires satisfying explicit instructions and implicit expectations about structure, appearance, and functionality. SpreadsheetArena evaluates this end-to-end task through blind comparisons between pairs of generated workbooks. The approach allows evaluators to judge complete artifacts even when the criteria for a good spreadsheet are difficult to formalize in advance.

Spreadsheets offer a defined output structure but also involve interacting dimensions, including layout and interactivity. The study finds that the stylistic, structural, and functional properties associated with preferred workbooks vary meaningfully across prompts. This makes preference dependent on the particular use case rather than a single fixed idea of workbook quality.

Expert assessments of finance-oriented workbooks reveal that even highly ranked models do not reliably follow domain-specific best practices. The authors release prompts, generated workbooks, and preference votes alongside a live arena. These resources support research into how overall preferences relate to particular artifact features and help distinguish strong comparative rankings from dependable performance in a specialized domain.
icml-2026-spreadsheetarena-decomposing-p.tldr: SpreadsheetArena evaluates generated workbooks through blind preferences and finds that high rankings do not ensure alignment with finance best practices.

paragraphs: Red-teaming language models requires finding attacks that are both effective and diverse. Generative Flow Networks offer a distribution-matching approach to this search, but unstable training can cause them to concentrate on a narrow set of outputs. The paper identifies unstable rewards in red-teaming as a factor that accelerates this collapse and motivates a more stable learning objective.

Stable-GFN removes the need to estimate the GFlowNet normalization quantity Z by using pairwise comparisons. It also applies a robust masking method to handle noisy rewards. These changes address instability in the training signal while maintaining the optimal policy of the underlying GFlowNet formulation, preserving the intended search behavior.

A further fluency stabilizer helps prevent optimization from becoming trapped in solutions that generate gibberish. Across the evaluated settings, the authors report strong attack effectiveness and diversity alongside more stable training. The contribution combines changes to reward handling, normalization, and fluency so that the search can continue finding varied vulnerabilities instead of collapsing onto a narrow or incoherent output pattern.
icml-2026-stable-gflownet-toward-diverse.tldr: Stable-GFN uses pairwise comparisons, reward masking, and fluency stabilization to improve the stability and diversity of LLM red-teaming.

paragraphs: Synthetic data can make information available for machine learning without distributing the original records. However, a service that trains the synthetic-data generator may still require access to those private records. FHAIM addresses this trust requirement by enabling a marginal-based generator to be trained on encrypted tabular data, keeping the underlying data encrypted throughout processing.

The framework adapts the AIM synthetic-data algorithm to fully homomorphic encryption using new encryption-compatible protocols. Fully homomorphic computation protects the data while the provider processes it, while differential privacy governs what is released. These protections address different stages of the workflow: access during training and privacy guarantees associated with the released result.

The authors describe FHAIM as the first fully homomorphic framework for this form of generator training. Their empirical analysis finds that it preserves AIM’s performance while keeping runtimes feasible. The significance is a service workflow that can generate useful synthetic tabular data without requiring the data holder to expose private training records to the provider.
icml-2026-textttfhaim-fully-homomorphic-.tldr: FHAIM trains a synthetic tabular-data generator on encrypted records and provides differential privacy for release while preserving AIM’s reported performance.

paragraphs: A probabilistic prediction may need to satisfy hard algebraic constraints, such as a trajectory avoiding obstacles. Constrained maximum a posteriori inference seeks the most likely prediction among those that are allowed. This becomes difficult when the feasible region is nonconvex and the probability density lacks the shape properties that make optimization straightforward.

The paper first investigates conditions under which continuous constrained MAP inference can be performed exactly and efficiently. For the tractable class it identifies, the authors develop a scalable message-passing algorithm. The exactness and efficiency result is tied to those conditions rather than extending automatically to every nonconvex constrained prediction problem.

For more general cases, the authors propose interleaving two operations: dividing the domain into convex feasible regions and applying numerical constrained optimization. This explicitly incorporates the structure of the constraints into the search for a likely prediction. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show that both proposed approaches outperform constraint-agnostic baselines, supporting the value of exploiting feasible-region structure.
icml-2026-the-theory-and-practice-of-map.tldr: The paper identifies an exactly solvable class of constrained MAP problems and develops a structure-aware optimization strategy for broader nonconvex cases.

paragraphs: During reinforcement-learning post-training, language-model agents can spend seconds or minutes waiting for external tools while allocated GPUs sit idle. Repeated calls create an opportunity to reuse results, but the same call can produce different outputs after different prior interactions. A useful cache must therefore account for the environment state created by the agent’s history.

TVCACHE organizes observed tool-call sequences into a tree and uses longest-prefix matching to find reusable results. A cache hit requires the full tool history to match a previously executed sequence, which the framework uses to guarantee an identical environment state. This makes the sequence of interactions part of the lookup, rather than treating each tool invocation as an isolated request.

The authors evaluate the system on terminal tasks, SQL generation, and video understanding. They report cache hit rates up to 67% and reductions in median tool-call execution time of up to 6.9 times, without degrading reward accumulation during post-training. The results show how history-aware reuse can reduce a substantial waiting cost in agent training.
icml-2026-tvcache-a-tool-value-cache-for.tldr: TVCACHE reuses tool outputs only for matching interaction histories, reducing tool latency without degrading reward accumulation in the evaluated workloads.
